standard.title: Cause and Effect, Continuity and Change
standard.description: analyse cause and effect, and evaluate patterns of continuity and change
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse cause and effect and evaluate patterns of continuity and change in a Year 9 historical context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse cause and effect and evaluate patterns of continuity and change across the Year 10 History topics, using primary sources and sequential argument.

nodes.label: Cause and effect analysis
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can organise primary sources chronologically to support a historical argument about significant causes, and explain the links between key ideas, actions and individuals.
nodes.minimum_width: Organise at least three primary sources chronologically and use them to support an argument about a significant cause; explain the links between at least two key ideas, actions or individuals.
nodes.typical_width: Organise a range of primary sources in chronological order to support the development of a historical argument about significant causes; explain the links between the main ideas, actions and individuals of an event, drawing links between them by placing them in sequence — for example, sequencing the Freedom Rides campaigns in the USA and Australia, and explaining the links between the two campaigns; identify the various manifestations or effects of an event in different geographical locations, using interactive timelines.
wider: Apply cause and effect analysis to a long-run historical process studied in the course (e.g. the evolution of immigration policy from 1945 to the present), evaluating how causes and effects compound and interact across multiple decades
Construct a multi-layered causal analysis for a contested event studied in the course — distinguishing between immediate, underlying and enabling causes and evaluating the relative weight of each

response_modes.reason: The Freedom Rides comparison (USA and Australia) is the elaboration-supported example for practising sequential argument with multiple sources. Use it as a model for how to sequence evidence and draw explicit causal links before asking students to apply the skill to a different topic.

success_criteria: Organise at least three primary sources in chronological sequence to support a historical argument
Explain the causal links between at least two key ideas, actions or individuals in a historical event
Identify at least two effects of a historical event in different geographical locations or domains

nodes.label: Continuity and change patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate patterns of continuity and change across the period studied, distinguishing surface-level changes from deeper continuities.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one pattern of continuity and one of change across the period studied and evaluate the significance of each.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate patterns of continuity and change across the Year 10 History topics — distinguishing surface-level changes (e.g. new roles for women during wartime) from structural continuities (e.g. return to traditional roles after the war); evaluate the significance of continuities and changes for different groups; use timelines and chronological analysis to map patterns across the period.
wider: Apply continuity and change analysis to a topic where the pattern is genuinely ambiguous — such as the status of First Nations Australians across the 20th century, where significant legal changes coexist with persistent structural inequalities — evaluating what framework is most appropriate

Compare patterns of continuity and change for two different groups across the same period (e.g. women and First Nations Australians from 1945 to the present), examining whether the same period represents change or continuity differently for each group

response_modes.reason: Continuity and change analysis synthesises the historical knowledge of K04, K12, K13 (home front women's roles, women's movement, civil rights trajectories) into an evaluative historical judgment. Use it as a synthesis activity connecting the K-strand knowledge to the S-strand skills.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The continuity-and-change framework applied to First Nations rights — where legal changes coexist with persistent structural inequality — is a rich analytical challenge that rewards students who can distinguish formal recognition from substantive change. It directly prepares for S07 (contested interpretations).
success_criteria: Identify at least one pattern of continuity and one of change across the period studied
Evaluate the significance of each pattern identified, explaining what it reveals about the period
Distinguish a surface-level change from a deeper structural continuity, using a specific example
